standard.title: Measure length with informal units
standard.description: Measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare objects directly by length (AC9MFM01) and order objects by length using direct comparison (AC9M1M01). They have not yet iterated a unit along a length to produce a numerical measure, or reasoned about why units must be uniform and placed end-to-end.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students measure the length of shapes and objects using informal units, recognising that units need to be uniform and used end-to-end.

nodes.label: Iterate units end-to-end
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can measure the length of an object by placing informal units end-to-end and counting them, producing a numerical measurement.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure one object using a chosen informal unit placed end-to-end; count the units and record the measurement.
nodes.typical_width: Measure several objects using an informal unit (blocks, pop sticks) placed end-to-end; count and record each measurement; compare measurements to determine which object is longer; explain what end-to-end placement means.
wider: Measure the same object multiple times using the same unit, investigating whether the result is always the same and discussing what could cause variation.
Measure classroom features (door frame, table, corridor) using body-based units (footsteps, handspans) and record results, discussing how this connects to historical measurement practices.

response_modes.reason: Correctly placing units end-to-end without gaps or overlaps requires practice and physical care — it is a procedural skill that needs to become reliable before students can reason about unit consistency. Errors in placement directly undermine the validity of the measurement.

nodes.hinge_reason: Placement errors (gaps or overlaps) produce invalid measurements that undermine Node 2 — students who cannot iterate units accurately cannot meaningfully compare measurements or reason about why units must be uniform, because their measurements are not trustworthy to begin with.
success_criteria: Places informal units end-to-end without gaps or overlaps to measure a length.
Counts and records the number of units correctly.

nodes.label: Units must be uniform
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain why informal units need to be the same size (uniform) to produce a valid and comparable measurement.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure one object using two different-sized informal units; explain why the two measurements give different numbers.
nodes.typical_width: Measure the same object with two different informal units (e.g. pop sticks and pencils); compare the resulting numbers; explain why different units give different counts; articulate that larger units produce smaller numbers for the same length and vice versa.
wider: Explore historical body-based measurement units (handspan, cubit, pace) and investigate why non-uniform body units caused problems for trade and communication — connecting the historical reason for standard units to the Year 1 concept.
Compare measurements taken by different students using footsteps as the unit, explaining why results differ and what would make the measurements directly comparable.

response_modes.reason: Students frequently assume that different measurements must mean different lengths — they don't yet see that the unit is the variable. Using two different units on the same object, and comparing results across classmates using non-uniform personal units (footsteps), gives the contexts that make the uniformity principle vivid.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The uniformity principle is the conceptual foundation of all measurement — understanding that a measurement is a ratio of the measured quantity to the unit. Students who truly understand why units must be uniform have grasped the deep structure of measurement.
success_criteria: Measures the same object with two different units and correctly states both measurements.
Explains why the two measurements are different, referring to the size of the unit.

nodes.label: Compare using measurement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use informal-unit measurement to compare the length of two or more objects, stating how much longer one is than another.
nodes.minimum_width: Measure two objects with the same informal unit; state which is longer and by how many units.
nodes.typical_width: Measure and compare two or more objects using the same informal unit; state the length difference in units; explain why the same unit must be used for both to make a valid comparison; apply measurement comparison to practical contexts (does this object fit in this space?).
wider: Measure and compare lengths across a classroom investigation — designing a measurement challenge where the question requires comparing multiple objects using a chosen unit.
Investigate what happens to comparative measurements when a different unit is chosen — confirming that the ordering of lengths is preserved even when the unit changes.

response_modes.reason: Using measurement to compare requires students to apply unit iteration, count correctly, ensure uniformity, and interpret the result in context — all components of the descriptor operating together.

success_criteria: Measures two objects with the same informal unit and states which is longer.
States the difference in length in units and explains why the same unit was necessary for a valid comparison.
